Wesfarmers stock faces new policy test as gas bill heads to Senate
sum: Wesfarmers stock traded at 49.91 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 09:30 CET on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The latest policy development came on Wednesday, November 11, when an Australian Senate committee backed the federal government's domestic gas reservation plan.

The proposal would require liquefied natural gas exporters to retain up to 20 percent of their production for the Australian market. Reuters reported that the committee described the reform as important, while warning that the bill still has to pass the Senate.

The measure has already cleared Australia's House of Representatives. Its next step is an upper-house debate in which the governing Labor party needs support from either the conservative Coalition or the Greens. Both groups oppose parts of the current design, leaving the final rules open to change.

If passed, the scheme is scheduled to begin in January 2028. That timetable is six months later than the date originally proposed by the government, according to Reuters. The delay gives producers, industrial users and investors more time to assess the eventual obligations, but it also prolongs uncertainty over the policy framework.

Western Australia is included in the national plan even though the state already operates a domestic reservation system. The state arrangement requires exporters to offer 15 percent of production to the local market, with the obligation measured over the life of a project rather than every year.

The national proposal would create a different structure for domestic supply. Reuters said the government wants to generate a modest oversupply in order to ease shortages and high prices, while gas producers warn that forcing additional supply into the market could weaken incentives to invest in exploration and new production.

That conflict leaves the policy outcome more important than the committee recommendation itself. A bill that passes without major amendments could alter the regulatory setting for Australian gas supply, while a negotiated version could change the scope, timing or treatment of Western Australian producers.

Wesfarmers stock faces hurdles over Australia's gas reservation plan
sum: Australia's domestic gas reservation plan faces a difficult parliamentary path, adding a new policy variable for Wesfarmers and its gas-reliant industrial activities. The latest development was reported on Wednesday, November 11, by Australian Associated Press.

The federal government has proposed requiring domestic gas companies to reserve up to 20 percent of exports for Australian consumers. A Senate inquiry recommended that the upper house pass the plan, but opposition senators said they would not support the proposal without substantial changes.

The Coalition argued that the scheme could redistribute existing gas rather than encourage new production. Labor needs support from either the Coalition or the Greens to secure passage through the Senate, leaving the final design and timing uncertain.

The proposal has already been softened. A minimum domestic-use requirement was changed to a cap of 20 percent, while producers may undershoot the target with government approval. Existing overseas contracts would also remain unaffected under the current design.

For Wesfarmers, the policy debate matters because reliable and competitively priced gas is an operating consideration for its chemicals and fertiliser businesses. The final framework could influence contract visibility, supply planning and the conditions for future industrial investment, although the latest report contains no Wesfarmers earnings revision or transaction.

Investors should therefore focus on the next parliamentary steps rather than treat the proposal as a completed policy change. The debate is expected to return to Parliament later in November, with only two sitting weeks remaining before the end of the year.

Consumer confidence slump puts ASX retailers and discretionary stocks in focus
sum: Australian consumer-facing stocks are back in focus after confidence fell to a four-year low, raising fresh concerns about discretionary spending heading into the crucial Christmas trading period.

The Westpac–Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November from 80.4 in October, its weakest reading since late 2022, as higher interest rates, inflation and rising living costs weighed heavily on households.
The deterioration could have implications for ASX-listed retailers including JB Hi-Fi Ltd, Harvey Norman Holdings Ltd, Wesfarmers Ltd and other businesses exposed to discretionary household spending.
The pressure is most acute among consumers with a mortgage, where sentiment plunged 11.6% to a record low of 68.1.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA)’s latest 25-basis-point rate rise lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, its highest level in 18 years, adding further pressure to household budgets already strained by inflation of 4.3% and petrol prices approaching $2.40 a litre.
“Cost-of-living concerns remain front and centre,” Westpac head of Australian macro-forecasting Matthew Hassan said.
Around 72% of consumers surveyed after the RBA decision expect mortgage rates to rise again over the next 12 months.

Australian shares slip below 9,000 level as banks overshadow miners' gains
sum: Australian shares edged lower on Monday, slipping back below the 9,000 level, as losses in heavyweight banks outweighed gains in mining stocks.
The S&P/ASX 200 index fell 0.3% to 8,997 by 0005 GMT, after closing 0.5% lower on Friday.
Financials were the biggest drag on the benchmark, falling 0.8%, with all of the "Big Four" banks down between 0.3% and 2.1%.
ANZ Group lost 2.1% despite reporting a 31% jump in annual cash profit. The lender's common equity tier 1 ratio, a key measure of capital strength, fell to 12% at the end of the fiscal year.
Citi analysts said in a note that underlying organic capital generation was flat for the lender, though they expect it to improve as profitability rises and credit growth slows into fiscal 2027.

Rate-sensitive real estate and consumer discretionary stocks fell 1.6% and 1.1%, respectively. Data-centre landlord Goodman Group declined 1.2%, while top non-food conglomerate Wesfarmers slipped 1.1%.
Resources stocks, which account for roughly a quarter of the benchmark, rose 1.9% as iron ore prices held firm. Sector heavyweights BHP Group and Rio Tinto gained 1.5% and 0.8%, respectively.

The Reserve Bank of Australia statement said the Board increased the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 percent. Six members supported the move, while three voted to keep the rate at 4.60 percent.

The central bank said inflation was expected to remain elevated through much of 2027. It also said higher interest rates and falling housing prices and turnover were expected to weigh on household consumption.

Wesfarmers operates Bunnings, Kmart, Target and Officeworks alongside health, beauty and wellness businesses and industrial and resources operations. That diversification provides several earnings channels, but its major retail brands remain exposed to household budgets and housing activity.

The next signals for investors are trading updates covering customer traffic, comparable sales and margin protection. Management's acquisition stance is another factor to watch. Wesfarmers has previously described potential deals across retail, lithium and chemicals as selective and disciplined, making execution and capital allocation relevant alongside near-term retail momentum.

Best ASX Retail Stocks to Watch in 2027: 6 Australian Shares With Momentum
sum: It has been a mixed reality for Australian retailers in 2026. On the one hand, supermarkets are experiencing increased demand for everyday essentials, while discretionary retailers are facing more cautious shoppers who are selective about where and how they spend.

Australian investors interested in ASX retail stocks are exposed to businesses across the divide, from those selling groceries and electronics to fashion and home appliances. This guide explores top ASX retail stocks with positive outlooks in 2027, their unique business strengths, and the factors to consider before investing in their retail shares.
ASX retail stocks are shares of companies listed on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) that generate revenue from selling goods and services to direct consumers.

These businesses operate across different categories such as groceries, electronics, clothing, homewares, beauty products, sporting goods, wearables, and more. As such, the country's largest supermarket chains and home-focused brands dominate the industry.
From an investment standpoint, publicly-listed retail businesses are categorised into two broad segments:

- Consumer stable brands: These are companies that sell everyday goods for individuals and households. Examples are supermarkets and food distributors that people patronise daily for food, groceries, and other essentials regardless of broader economic conditions.

- Consumer discretionary brands: These retailers sell products that consumers may not consider spending on immediately, depending on their budgets. Any product a consumer can postpone buying or spend less on due to interest rates, wages, employment conditions, and consumer confidence falls in this category. They include electronics, fashion items, furniture, and sporting goods.

Our view after Coles’ shares plunge
sum: Shares dropped 8% after reporting results for the September 2026 quarter.

Coles’ (ASX: COL) shares fell 8% after it reported core supermarket sales growth of 4% in the September 2026 quarter, similar to the growth achieved in the June 2026 quarter. Liquor sales declined 1% in the quarter, but sales momentum is improving.

Why it matters: Coles is underperforming archrival Woolworths, whose Australian supermarkets grew nearly twice as fast during the September quarter. We expect Coles to defend market share at the expense of profitability over the year.
- Guidance for flat first-half Supermarkets EBIT would preclude margin expansion, which we believe the market was expecting. We leave our flat EBIT margin forecast unchanged for fiscal 2027.

- The liquor segment continues to face headwinds from lower alcohol consumption, though sales declines are moderating. Even so, Coles is still losing share to industry leader Endeavour, whose sales grew 3% in the quarter.

The bottom line: We trim our fiscal 2027 sales forecast, but our earnings estimates are broadly unchanged, and we maintain our fair value estimate for no-moat Coles at $16.50 per share. Shares remain materially overvalued despite the fall following the September quarter update.

- Coles underperformed Woolworths over the past 12 months, but we expect it to match Woolworths’ deliberate discounting to reinvigorate sales momentum. Coles is flagging more discounts to boost sales, but we expect Woolworths to follow suit in real time.

Investing in ASX consumer discretionary shares in 2026
sum: The consumer discretionary sector is a subset of the retail industry. Retailers are businesses that sell products or services to end consumers. That is in contrast to wholesalers that sell goods to other companies, usually in large quantities. Retailers often purchase goods from wholesalers or suppliers and then resell those items directly to the public for profit.

Consumer discretionary items include luxury and high-end products and services like designer brand handbags, electronic devices, and even holidays. In contrast, consumer staples are basic essentials like everyday food items and healthcare products. We like to splurge on consumer discretionary products when we have extra disposable income, whereas consumer staples are the bare necessities we usually can't get by without.

The performance of consumer discretionary stocks is closely tied to the health of Australian household finances — and the picture heading into 2026 is a mixed one. The S&P/ASX 200 Consumer Discretionary Index (ASX: XDJ) increased 1.77% and produced total returns of 4.09% in 2025, a modest result compared to other sectors. The index hit an all-time high of 4,620 points in August 20251, before giving back some of those gains as macroeconomic headwinds mounted.

A key driver of the sector's performance has been the RBA's monetary policy cycle. The Reserve Bank of Australia lifted its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.1% at its March 2026 meeting, following a hike in February amid renewed inflationary pressures in the second half of 20252. Higher interest rates increase borrowing costs and strain household budgets — particularly for mortgage holders — leaving less income available for the non-essential spending that consumer discretionary companies rely on.

That said, there are genuine bright spots. RBA Governor Michele Bullock noted in late 2025 that Australian consumers were starting to spend more as disposable incomes and wealth climbed. Timely indicators pointed to continued growth in household consumption, with retail contacts reporting a modest uplift in underlying retail demand. For investors, this means consumer discretionary stocks remain a sector that rewards patience and careful stock selection, particularly in a rate-sensitive environment.

Australia's Wesfarmers shares slide despite forecast-beating $1.1 billion profit
sum: Feb 19 (Reuters) - Wesfarmers, Australia's biggest non-food retailer, on Thursday warned of uneven consumer spending as its second-half sales growth missed expectations, sending its shares down by their most in over three months despite a forecast-beating first-half profit.

Wesfarmers, which owns the country's most popular hardware chain Bunnings, and discount retailer Kmart, posted a 9.3% rise in its interim net profit after tax to A$1.6 billion ($1.13 billion), beating the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of A$1.56 billion.
CEO Rob Scott said consumer demand had been "solid" so far for the second half, with sales in line with the first half, but higher costs were weighing on consumers unevenly.
He warned the uncertain outlooks for inflation and interest rates were also affecting consumer sentiment and spending.
"Inflation is arguably one of the major challenges for the Australian economy because it is impacting the cost of living," he told reporters.
"The problem with inflation is, although it's felt broadly across the economy, it is also felt somewhat unevenly. So it is lower-income families that bear the brunt of it."

Australia's underlying inflation picked up to 3.4% last quarter, the fastest pace in over a year. That prompted the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise rates for the first time in two years by 25 basis points to 3.85% in a unanimous decision this month.
